tech-ai-engineer.title: AI engineer path
tech-ai-engineer.description: From the maths behind machine learning to classical ML, deep learning, transformers and large language models — prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, evaluation, MLOps and responsible AI.

courses.title: Maths for machine learning (only what you need, fully explained)
courses.summary: Vectors, dot products, matrices, derivatives, gradient descent, probability and Bayes' rule — explained from school maths upward, always tied to how ML models actually use them.
outcomes: Learners can compute dot products, norms and cosine similarity and explain why embeddings use them
Learners can multiply matrices and see a neural-network layer as a matrix operation
Learners can use derivatives and the chain rule to perform gradient descent by hand
Learners can apply conditional probability and Bayes' rule, and interpret mean, variance and the normal distribution

story.title: How Asha's music app knew her taste

scenes.text: Asha, a college student in Guwahati, noticed her music app kept suggesting songs she loved. She asked her friend Vikram, a data scientist, how.
Vikram drew two arrows on a napkin: 'Each song is a list of numbers — energy, tempo, acousticness and so on. That list is a vector.'
'Songs whose arrows point in a similar direction feel similar. We measure that with the dot product and the angle between them.'
Asha realised that the same idea powers search engines and AI chatbots that 'understand' meaning.

steps.title: Vectors
steps.body:
A **vector** is an ordered list of numbers, e.g. a = (3, 4). Geometrically it is an arrow from the origin.
- **Length (norm):** ‖a‖ = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.
- **Addition:** (3, 4) + (1, 2) = (4, 6) — add position by position.
- **Scaling:** 2 × (3, 4) = (6, 8).
In ML, a vector can describe a house (area, rooms, age), a pixel patch, or the *meaning* of a word or sentence (an **embedding** with hundreds of dimensions).

steps.title: Dot product
steps.body:
a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + … + aₙbₙ
Example: (3, 4) · (4, 3) = 12 + 12 = 24.

Geometric meaning: a · b = ‖a‖ ‖b‖ cos θ, where θ is the angle between them.
- Large positive → pointing the same way.
- Zero → perpendicular (unrelated).
- Negative → opposite directions.

steps.title: Worked example: cosine similarity
steps.body:
cos θ = (a · b) ÷ (‖a‖ ‖b‖)
Song A = (0.9, 0.1), Song B = (0.8, 0.2), Song C = (0.1, 0.9) [energy, calmness].
- A·B = 0.72 + 0.02 = 0.74; ‖A‖ ≈ 0.906, ‖B‖ ≈ 0.825 → cos ≈ 0.99 (very similar).
- A·C = 0.09 + 0.09 = 0.18; ‖C‖ ≈ 0.906 → cos ≈ 0.22 (different).
Cosine similarity ranges from −1 to 1 and ignores length, so it compares *direction* — the 'kind' of thing. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems use this to find relevant passages.

steps.title: Why ML loves dot products
steps.body: A single artificial neuron computes w · x + b: a dot product of weights and inputs plus a bias. Attention in transformers compares a query vector with key vectors using dot products. GPUs are built to do enormous numbers of these multiply-adds in parallel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dot products require vectors of the **same length**.
- The dot product is a **number**, not a vector.
- Forgetting to normalise: a long vector may have a larger dot product with everything simply because it is long; cosine similarity fixes this.
- Mixing units (rupees and square feet) without scaling features distorts distances.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Compute the cosine similarity of (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6). Before calculating, predict the answer. (Hint: one is exactly twice the other.)

activity.prompt: Compute the dot product (2, −1, 3) · (4, 5, 1).

quiz.why: The norm is the vector's length: √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. Do not add the components or multiply them.
The dot product is 1×0 + 0×1 = 0. A dot product of 0 means the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).

quiz.q: Cosine similarity of (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6)?
quiz.why: (2, 4, 6) is 2 times (1, 2, 3), so the vectors point in the same direction. Cosine similarity depends only on direction, so cos θ = 1.

quiz.q: An artificial neuron's core computation is…
quiz.why: A neuron computes the weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, w·x + b, and then applies an activation function.

quiz.q: Why use cosine similarity instead of raw dot product for documents?
options: It ignores vector length and compares direction
quiz.why: Cosine similarity compares direction, not length. For documents, a long document would otherwise have a large dot product just because it has more words.

lessons.title: Matrices: many dot products at once

scenes.text: Pooja, a property analyst in Pune, had a spreadsheet: 1,000 houses (rows) × 3 features (area, rooms, age).
To estimate prices, her model multiplied each row by weights. Her colleague Ben said: 'That spreadsheet is a matrix. One matrix multiplication prices all 1,000 houses in one go.'

steps.title: What is a matrix?
steps.body: A **matrix** is a rectangular grid of numbers with m rows and n columns (an m × n matrix). Your dataset is usually a matrix X: each row is one example, each column one feature. A greyscale image is a matrix of pixel brightness.

steps.title: Matrix multiplication
steps.body:
To multiply A (m × n) by B (n × p), the inner sizes must match (n = n). The result is m × p.
Entry (i, j) = dot product of row i of A with column j of B.

Example: A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], B = [[5], [6]]
- Row 1: 1×5 + 2×6 = 17
- Row 2: 3×5 + 4×6 = 39
AB = [[17], [39]]

steps.title: Transpose and identity
steps.body:
- **Transpose** Aᵀ flips rows and columns: a 2 × 3 becomes 3 × 2.
- **Identity** I has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere: AI = A.
- Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: AB is usually not equal to BA (and one may not even be defined).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shape errors: the most common bug in ML code. Always write the shapes next to each line, e.g. (batch 32 × 784) @ (784 × 128) → (32 × 128).
- Confusing element-wise multiplication (A * B in NumPy) with matrix multiplication (A @ B).
- Assuming AB = BA.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Multiply [[2, 0], [1, 3]] by [[1, 4], [2, 5]] (answer: [[2, 8], [7, 19]]). Then multiply in the other order (answer: [[6, 12], [9, 15]]) and confirm the answers differ.

statements.s: A (3 × 4) matrix can be multiplied by a (4 × 2) matrix.
statements.why: Inner sizes (4 and 4) match; the result is 3 × 2.

statements.s: The transpose of a 2 × 5 matrix is 5 × 2.
In NumPy, A * B is matrix multiplication.
Each entry of AB is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B.

quiz.why: For a matrix product (a × b)@(b × c), the inner sizes (784) must match, and the result takes the outer sizes: 32 × 10.
Each output row is the dot product of the row with (1, 1): 1×1 + 2×1 = 3 and 3×1 + 4×1 = 7. So the result is [[3], [7]].

quiz.q: In a dataset matrix, a row usually represents…
quiz.why: In a dataset matrix, each row is one example (sample) and each column is a feature.

quiz.q: Most common bug when writing ML code by hand?
quiz.why: Shape mismatch is the most common bug when writing ML code by hand. Tracking the shape of each array at every step catches it early.

quiz.q: AI (A times the identity) equals…
quiz.why: The identity matrix I leaves any matrix unchanged under multiplication, so AI = A.

story.title: Rahul walks down a foggy hill

scenes.text: On a trek near Munnar, fog rolled in. Guide Rahul told his group: 'We can't see the valley, but we can feel the slope under our feet. Step downhill, again and again.'
One trekker, Mira, an ML engineer, laughed: 'That's exactly how we train neural networks. It's called gradient descent.'

steps.title: Derivative = slope
steps.body:
The **derivative** f′(x) tells how fast f changes when x changes a tiny bit — the slope of the curve at x.
Rules you will use constantly:
- d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹ → d/dx (x²) = 2x
- d/dx (constant) = 0
- d/dx (a·f) = a·f′
- d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ;  d/dx (ln x) = 1/x
For functions of many variables, the **gradient** ∇f is the vector of partial derivatives — it points in the direction of steepest *increase*.

steps.title: Gradient descent
steps.body:
Training a model = finding weights w that make a **loss** L(w) (error) as small as possible.
Repeat:
w ← w − η · ∇L(w)
- η (eta) is the **learning rate** — the step size.
- We subtract because the gradient points uphill and we want to go down.

steps.title: Worked example by hand
steps.body:
Minimise L(w) = (w − 3)². Derivative: L′(w) = 2(w − 3). Start w = 0, η = 0.1.
- Step 1: grad = 2(0 − 3) = −6 → w = 0 − 0.1 × (−6) = 0.6
- Step 2: grad = 2(0.6 − 3) = −4.8 → w = 0.6 + 0.48 = 1.08
- Step 3: grad = −3.84 → w = 1.464
Each step closes 20% of the remaining gap; w approaches 3, the true minimum.

steps.title: Chain rule = backpropagation
steps.body:
If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x).
Example: y = (2x + 1)². Let u = 2x + 1: dy/du = 2u, du/dx = 2, so dy/dx = 4(2x + 1).
A neural network is a long chain of functions; **backpropagation** applies the chain rule from the output backwards to get the gradient for every weight efficiently.

steps.title: Learning-rate pitfalls
steps.body:
- **Too large:** steps overshoot and the loss bounces or explodes (for L = (w−3)², any η above 1 diverges).
- **Too small:** training crawls.
- Real losses have flat regions and saddle points; optimisers like momentum and **Adam** adapt the steps. **Stochastic** gradient descent uses small random batches of data per step, which is faster and adds helpful noise.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Repeat the worked example with η = 0.5. How many steps does it take to reach w = 3? (Answer: one! Because 0 − 0.5 × (−6) = 3.) Then try η = 1.0 and see what happens: w jumps between 0 and 6 forever.

bands.text: Very small: safe but slow — many steps to converge.
Healthy: the loss shrinks smoothly every step (at exactly 0.5 this simple bowl is solved in one step).
Large: w overshoots and oscillates around 3, but still converges.
Exactly 1.0: w bounces between two values forever.
Too large: each step overshoots further — training diverges.

quiz.q: d/dx (x³) = ?
quiz.why: By the power rule d/dx(xⁿ) = n·xⁿ⁻¹. So d/dx(x³) = 3x².

quiz.q: In gradient descent we move…
quiz.why: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss. Gradient descent moves opposite to it, to reduce the loss.
The gradient is 2(w − 3) = 2(1 − 3) = −4. The update is w − η·grad = 1 − 0.25×(−4) = 1 + 1 = 2.

quiz.q: Backpropagation is an application of…
quiz.why: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute derivatives through the layers, one layer after another.

quiz.q: Loss keeps increasing wildly during training. First suspect?
quiz.why: If loss keeps increasing wildly, the learning rate is probably too high, so each step overshoots the minimum. Check it first before anything else.

lessons.title: Probability, Bayes and the statistics of data

scenes.text: A screening test for a rare condition is '99% accurate'. Dr. Nandini in Chandigarh explained to a worried patient, Mr. Gill, why a positive result did not mean he was 99% likely to have it.
She drew 10,000 people. 1 in 1,000 has the condition: 10 people. The test catches 99% of them (about 10) but also wrongly flags 1% of the 9,990 healthy people — about 100.
So of ~110 positives, only ~10 are true. Mr. Gill's chance was about 9%, not 99%. He went for a confirmatory test, calmer.

steps.title: Probability basics
steps.body:
- P(A) is between 0 and 1.
- P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
- Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Two coin heads: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.
- **Conditional probability:** P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) — the probability of A *given* B happened.

steps.title: Bayes' rule
steps.body:
P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) ÷ P(E)
- P(H): **prior** — belief before evidence (prevalence 0.001).
- P(E | H): **likelihood** — how likely the evidence if H is true (sensitivity 0.99).
- P(E): total probability of the evidence = P(E|H)P(H) + P(E|not H)P(not H) = 0.99×0.001 + 0.01×0.999 ≈ 0.01098.
- P(H | E) ≈ 0.00099 ÷ 0.01098 ≈ **0.09**.
This is why **base rates** matter. Spam filters (Naive Bayes) and many ML ideas use this rule.

steps.title: Describing data
steps.body:
- **Mean** (average), **median** (middle value — robust to outliers), **mode** (most common).
- **Variance** = average squared distance from the mean; **standard deviation** σ = √variance.
- **Normal distribution:** bell-shaped; about 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ of the mean.
Example: salaries 30k, 32k, 35k, 400k — mean ≈ 124k but median = 33.5k. The median tells the truer story here.

steps.title: Where this appears in ML
steps.body:
- Classifiers output probabilities (e.g. P(spam | email) = 0.93).
- **Softmax** turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1.
- **Cross-entropy loss** punishes confident wrong probabilities.
- Language models predict a probability for every possible next token.
- Evaluation: precision and recall are conditional probabilities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A)** — the 'prosecutor's fallacy'.
- Ignoring base rates (as above).
- Assuming independence when events are linked (rain and traffic).
- Treating correlation as causation: ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: A spam filter: 20% of email is spam. The word 'lottery' appears in 40% of spam and 1% of normal email. If an email contains 'lottery', what is P(spam)? (Answer: 0.4×0.2 ÷ (0.4×0.2 + 0.01×0.8) = 0.08 ÷ 0.088 ≈ 0.91.)

activity.prompt: Bayes: prevalence 2%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 5%. P(condition | positive) in % (nearest whole number)?

quiz.q: P(not A) if P(A) = 0.3?
quiz.why: By the complement rule, P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

quiz.q: Two independent events each 0.5. Both happen?
quiz.why: For independent events, multiply the probabilities: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.

quiz.q: Data with one huge outlier: best 'typical' value?
quiz.why: The median resists outliers because it only depends on the middle value. A huge outlier pulls the mean up, but it does not change the median much.

quiz.q: In a normal distribution, roughly what % lies within 2 standard deviations?
quiz.why: The 68–95–99.7 rule says about 68% lies within 1 standard deviation, about 95% within 2 and about 99.7% within 3.

quiz.q: Why was Mr. Gill's chance only ~9%?
options: The condition is rare, so false positives outnumber true positives
quiz.why: When a condition is rare, most people are healthy. So even a small false-positive rate gives more false positives than true positives, which pulls P(disease | positive) down. Bayes' rule is correct; the base rate is the cause.

questions.q: A vector is…
questions.why: A vector is an ordered list of numbers (or an arrow with direction and length). A single number is a scalar.

questions.q: Derivative of a constant?
questions.why: The derivative of a constant is 0, because a constant does not change as x changes.
Dot product = 1×3 + 2×4 = 3 + 8 = 11. The result is a single number, not a vector.

questions.q: (2 × 3) @ (3 × 5) has shape…
questions.why: For (2 × 3)@(3 × 5), the inner 3s match and the result has the outer sizes: 2 × 5.

questions.q: Gradient descent update?
questions.why: Gradient descent steps against the gradient: w ← w − η∇L. Adding it would increase the loss.

questions.q: d/dx (5x²) = ?
Median of 3, 9, 1, 7, 100?
questions.why: Sort the numbers: 1, 3, 7, 9, 100. The middle value is 7. The mean (24) is pulled up by the outlier 100.

questions.q: y = (3x − 1)². dy/dx?
questions.why: Use the chain rule: the derivative of the outer square is 2(3x − 1) and of the inner part is 3. So dy/dx = 2(3x − 1) × 3 = 6(3x − 1).

questions.q: Cosine similarity of (1, 0) and (−1, 0)?
questions.why: (−1, 0) points the opposite way to (1, 0), so the angle is 180° and cos θ = −1.
The gradient is 2(w − 5) = 2(1 − 5) = −8. The update is 1 − 0.1×(−8) = 1 + 0.8 = 1.8.

questions.q: Prevalence 1%, sensitivity 100%, false-positive rate 1%. P(disease | positive)?
questions.why: Take 10,000 people: 100 have the disease and all test positive. Among the 9,900 healthy, 1% (99) test positive. So P = 100/(100 + 99) ≈ 50%.

questions.q: Why does a learning rate of 1.0 make w oscillate forever for L = (w−3)²?
options: Each step exactly overshoots to the mirror point
questions.why: With η = 1 the update is w − 2(w − 3) = 6 − w, which flips w to the mirror point about 3. So w jumps back and forth and never converges, unless it starts exactly at 3.

questions.q: Softmax outputs…
questions.why: Softmax turns raw scores into a probability distribution: every output is non-negative and the outputs sum to 1.

courses.title: Classical machine learning
courses.summary: How machines learn from data: problem framing, train/validation/test splits, linear and logistic regression, decision trees and ensembles, clustering, and honest evaluation with the right metrics.
outcomes: Learners can frame a business problem as regression, classification or clustering
Learners can split data correctly and avoid leakage
Learners can explain and apply linear/logistic regression, trees, random forests, gradient boosting, k-NN and k-means
Learners can choose metrics such as precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and RMSE and diagnose over/underfitting

lessons.title: Framing ML problems and preparing data

scenes.text: Divya leads analytics at a telecom company in Mumbai. Each month thousands of prepaid customers stop recharging (they 'churn').
Her manager asked: 'Can AI tell us who will leave next month?' Divya first asked: what exactly will we predict, from what data, and what will we do with the prediction?
She defined: label = no recharge in the next 30 days; features = last 3 months of usage, recharges, complaints; action = targeted offers to the riskiest 5%.
Only then did she open a modelling notebook.

steps.title: Types of ML
steps.body:
- **Supervised learning:** examples come with the right answer (label). *Regression* predicts a number (house price); *classification* predicts a category (churn yes/no, spam/not spam).
- **Unsupervised learning:** no labels; find structure — *clustering* customers into groups, *dimensionality reduction*.
- **Reinforcement learning:** an agent learns by trial, error and reward (game playing, robotics).
- **Self-supervised learning:** labels come from the data itself (predict the next word) — the basis of large language models.

steps.title: Train, validation, test
steps.body:
- **Training set** (e.g. 70%): the model learns from it.
- **Validation set** (15%): you compare models and tune settings (hyperparameters).
- **Test set** (15%): touched **once** at the end for an honest estimate.
**Cross-validation** (k-fold) rotates the validation part across k folds for a more stable estimate on small data.
For time-dependent data (churn, sales), split by **time**: train on the past, test on the future.

steps.title: Data leakage — the silent killer
steps.body:
Leakage = information in training that would not be available at prediction time.
Examples:
- Using 'account closed date' to predict churn (it only exists after churn!).
- Scaling or imputing using statistics computed on the *whole* dataset before splitting.
- The same customer appearing in both train and test.
Symptom: amazing validation scores, poor real-world results.

steps.title: Feature preparation
steps.body:
- **Missing values:** impute (median, a 'missing' flag) or drop — and understand *why* they are missing.
- **Categorical features:** one-hot encode (city → is_Mumbai, is_Delhi…) or target-encode carefully.
- **Scaling:** standardise (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) for distance- or gradient-based models (k-NN, logistic regression, neural nets). Trees do not need it.
- **Class imbalance:** if only 3% churn, accuracy is misleading; use suitable metrics, class weights or resampling — on training data only.

steps.title: Worked example: a scikit-learn pipeline
steps.body:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced'))
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)          # scaler learns mean/std from TRAIN only
print(model.score(X_te, y_te))

The pipeline prevents the classic scaling leak. stratify keeps the churn proportion equal in both splits.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick a decision you see every day (a food app's delivery-time estimate, a bank's loan approval). Write: the label, 5 features available *at decision time*, the type of ML problem, and one feature that would be leakage.

activity.prompt: Classify each problem.

items.text: Predict tomorrow's electricity demand in MW
Is this transaction fraudulent?
Group shoppers by behaviour with no labels
Estimate a flat's rent
Which of 5 crop diseases is in this leaf photo?
Find natural segments of news articles

quiz.q: Which set should be used only once, at the end?
quiz.why: The test set should be used only once, at the end. If you keep checking it and adjusting your model, it leaks into your decisions and no longer gives an honest estimate.

quiz.q: Data leakage means…
options: Training uses information unavailable at prediction time
quiz.why: Data leakage is when training uses information that would not be available at prediction time. It inflates offline scores, but the model fails in real use.

quiz.q: Which model does NOT need feature scaling?
quiz.why: A decision tree splits on thresholds, so changing the scale of a feature does not change the splits. k-NN, neural networks and regularised models are all sensitive to scale.

quiz.q: Predicting the price of a used car is…
quiz.why: The price is a continuous number, so predicting it is regression. Classification would predict a category.

quiz.q: For monthly churn data, the best split is…
options: By time: past for training, later months for testing
quiz.why: For monthly data over time, split by time: train on the past and test on later months. A random shuffle would let the model see the future, which is not how it will be used.

scenes.text: Bishnu manages a tea estate near Jorhat. He wondered how rainfall and fertiliser affect yield per hectare.
His daughter Anjali, a statistics student, fitted a linear regression: yield ≈ w₁·rain + w₂·fertiliser + b. The weights showed each factor's average association with yield.
Next season they wanted 'Will this section get blister blight: yes or no?' — a classification problem. Anjali switched to logistic regression, which outputs a probability.

steps.title: Linear regression
steps.body:
Prediction: ŷ = w · x + b.
Training minimises **mean squared error**: MSE = average of (y − ŷ)².
One feature example: data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) → best line ŷ = 2x (w = 2, b = 0), MSE = 0.
Interpretation: each weight is the expected change in y for a one-unit change in that feature, *holding other features fixed* — an association, not proof of causation.

steps.title: Logistic regression
steps.body:
For yes/no, pass the linear score z = w · x + b through the **sigmoid**: σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)).
- z = 0 → 0.5; large positive z → near 1; large negative → near 0.
- Predict 'yes' if σ(z) ≥ a **threshold** (0.5 by default, but you choose it based on costs).
Training minimises **log loss (cross-entropy)**, which heavily punishes confident wrong answers. Despite its name, logistic regression is a classifier.

steps.title: Worked example: one prediction
steps.body:
Spam model: z = 1.5 × (count of 'free') − 2.
Email with 'free' twice: z = 3 − 2 = 1 → σ(1) ≈ 0.73 → spam at threshold 0.5.
Email with 'free' once: z = −0.5 → σ ≈ 0.38 → not spam.
Change the threshold to 0.8 and even the first email passes as not-spam — fewer false alarms, more missed spam.

steps.title: Regularisation
steps.body:
Models with many features can fit noise. **Regularisation** adds a penalty for large weights:
- **L2 (ridge):** penalty Σw² — shrinks weights smoothly.
- **L1 (lasso):** penalty Σ|w| — can push weights to exactly zero (built-in feature selection).
The strength (λ, or C = 1/λ in scikit-learn) is a hyperparameter tuned on validation data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading weights as causes. Correlated features (rainfall and humidity) can split or flip weights.
- Fitting a straight line to a clearly curved relationship — add polynomial or interaction features, or use a non-linear model.
- Forgetting to scale features before regularised regression (the penalty becomes unfair across units).
- Using 0.5 as threshold when false negatives are far costlier (missing a disease vs. an extra test).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Data: (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7), (4, 9). Guess w and b for ŷ = wx + b, then check that MSE is 0. (Answer: w = 2, b = 1.) Then compute σ(0) = 0.5, σ(2) ≈ 0.88 and σ(−2) ≈ 0.12.

activity.prompt: Match each idea to its description.
pairs: Can drive weights exactly to zero

quiz.q: Logistic regression is used for…
quiz.why: Despite its name, logistic regression is used for classification. It outputs the probability of a class using the sigmoid function.
Check the points: 2×1 + 1 = 3, 2×2 + 1 = 5, 2×3 + 1 = 7. All fit, so the line is ŷ = 2x + 1.

quiz.q: Which regularisation can perform feature selection?
quiz.why: L1 (lasso) regularisation can shrink some weights to exactly zero, which removes those features. L2 (ridge) only shrinks the weights.

quiz.q: Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 generally…
options: Reduces false positives but may miss more positives
quiz.why: A higher threshold means the model says 'yes' only when more sure. So there are fewer false positives, but more real positives are missed.

story.title: Loan decisions at a cooperative bank

scenes.text: At a cooperative bank in Nashik, loan officer Sunita wanted a model the board could understand. A decision tree did that: 'If income < 25k and existing EMIs > 40% of income → high risk.'
But a single tree changed a lot when data changed slightly. Data scientist Farhan trained a random forest — hundreds of trees voting — and later gradient boosting, which was most accurate.
For marketing, they used k-means to group members into segments without any labels.

steps.title: Decision trees
steps.body:
A tree asks a series of yes/no questions on features. At each node it picks the split that makes the groups **purest** (lowest Gini impurity or entropy for classification; lowest variance for regression).
- Pros: easy to explain, handles mixed data, no scaling.
- Cons: a deep tree memorises noise (overfits). Control it with max_depth, min_samples_leaf.

steps.title: Ensembles
steps.body:
- **Bagging / Random forest:** train many trees on random bootstrap samples, each split considering a random subset of features; average or vote. Reduces variance; a robust default.
- **Boosting** (gradient boosting — e.g. XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost): build trees one after another, each correcting the previous errors. Often the strongest choice for tabular (spreadsheet-like) data; needs careful tuning (learning rate, number of trees, depth) and early stopping.

steps.title: k-nearest neighbours (k-NN)
steps.body: To classify a new point, look at the k closest training points and take a majority vote (or average for regression). Simple, no real training phase, but slow at prediction on big data and sensitive to scaling and irrelevant features. k is chosen by validation: small k is noisy, large k is too smooth.

steps.title: Worked example: k-means by hand
steps.body:
Points on a line: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12. k = 2; start centroids at 1 and 2.
- Assign: {1} near 1; {2, 3, 10, 11, 12} near 2.
- Update: centroids → 1 and 7.6.
- Assign: {1, 2, 3} near 1 (3 is 2 away from 1, 4.6 from 7.6); {10, 11, 12} near 7.6.
- Update: centroids → 2 and 11. Assign again: no change → converged.
k-means needs you to choose k (elbow method, silhouette score) and assumes roughly round, similar-sized clusters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using k-NN or k-means without scaling — income in lakhs swamps age in years.
- Trusting a single deep tree's high training accuracy.
- Reading random-forest 'feature importance' as causation; impurity-based importance also favours features with many unique values — permutation importance or SHAP values are more reliable.
- In lending, using features that act as proxies for protected characteristics. Check fairness (see Responsible AI).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw a 2-level decision tree by hand that decides 'play cricket today?' from outlook (sunny/rainy) and humidity (high/normal). Then ask: what extra data would make it fairer and more accurate?

items.back: Many de-correlated trees on bootstrap samples; average/vote. Lowers variance.
Trees added sequentially to fix previous errors. Often best on tabular data.
How mixed the classes are in a node: 0 = pure.
Number of neighbours that vote; tuned on validation data.
Number of clusters you ask for; choose with elbow/silhouette.
Stop adding trees/epochs when validation error stops improving.

quiz.q: A node with all examples of one class has Gini impurity…
quiz.why: A node with all examples of one class is perfectly pure, so its Gini impurity is 0. The maximum for two classes is 0.5.

quiz.q: Random forests mainly reduce…
quiz.why: A random forest averages many different trees, which cancels their individual noise. This mainly reduces variance (overfitting), not bias.

quiz.q: Boosting builds trees…
quiz.why: Boosting builds trees one after another, each fixing the errors of the previous ones. Random forests build trees independently in parallel.

quiz.q: k-means is…
quiz.why: k-means is unsupervised: it groups data into clusters without any labels.

quiz.q: Why scale features before k-NN?
options: Distances are dominated by large-unit features otherwise
quiz.why: k-NN uses distances. Without scaling, a feature with large units (like salary) dominates the distance and the small-unit features are ignored.

lessons.title: Evaluation: metrics, overfitting and honest results

story.title: The 97% accurate fraud model that caught nothing

scenes.text: A fintech start-up in Bengaluru proudly announced a fraud model with 97% accuracy. Risk head Kavya asked one question: 'What percentage of transactions are fraud?'
Answer: 3%. A model saying 'not fraud' to everything would also be 97% accurate. Their model, it turned out, caught almost no fraud.
Kavya replaced accuracy with precision, recall and PR-AUC, chose a threshold based on the cost of each mistake, and the real work began.

steps.title: The confusion matrix
steps.body:
For a yes/no classifier:
- **TP** true positive: fraud, flagged.
- **FP** false positive: genuine, flagged (annoys customer).
- **FN** false negative: fraud, missed (loses money).
- **TN** true negative: genuine, passed.
Metrics:
- Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — of the flagged, how many were truly fraud?
- **Recall** (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN) — of all fraud, how much did we catch?
- **F1** = 2PR / (P + R) — balance of the two.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1,000 transactions, 30 fraud. Model flags 40: 24 truly fraud.
- TP = 24, FP = 16, FN = 6, TN = 954.
- Precision = 24/40 = 0.60; Recall = 24/30 = 0.80.
- F1 = 2 × 0.6 × 0.8 / 1.4 ≈ 0.686.
- Accuracy = 978/1000 = 97.8% — sounds great but hides the trade-off.

steps.title: Threshold-free metrics and regression metrics
steps.body:
- **ROC-AUC:** probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative (0.5 = random, 1 = perfect).
- **PR-AUC** (average precision): more informative when positives are rare.
- Regression: **MAE** (average absolute error, easy to explain), **RMSE** (punishes big errors more), **R²** (share of variance explained).
Always compare with a **baseline** (predict the mean; predict the majority class).

steps.title: Overfitting, underfitting, bias–variance
steps.body:
- **Underfitting (high bias):** poor on train and validation — model too simple. Add features or capacity.
- **Overfitting (high variance):** great on train, poor on validation — memorising. Get more data, regularise, simplify, use early stopping.
- **Learning curves** (score vs. training-set size) show which problem you have.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
- Tuning on the test set ('just one more peek').
- Comparing models on different splits.
- Ignoring uncertainty: a 0.5% gain on 200 test examples is likely noise.
- Forgetting the business: choose the threshold where (cost of FP × count) + (cost of FN × count) is lowest.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: A cancer screening model has recall 0.99 and precision 0.10. Explain in plain words what that means, and why doctors might still accept it as a first-stage screen followed by a more precise test.

a.text: You are Kavya. The team's new fraud model has ROC-AUC 0.93. The CEO wants it live tomorrow at threshold 0.5. What do you ask first?

choices.label: What precision and recall do we get at that threshold on recent, untouched data?
choices.feedback: Right — AUC alone does not tell you the operating point.

choices.label: Nothing, 0.93 is excellent
choices.feedback: AUC summarises all thresholds; the business lives at one threshold.

b.text: At 0.5: precision 0.30, recall 0.85. Support says each false alarm costs Rs 50 in calls; each missed fraud costs Rs 4,000 on average. What next?

choices.label: Pick the threshold that minimises total expected cost on validation data
choices.feedback: Exactly — let money and customer impact decide.

choices.label: Raise the threshold until precision is 0.9 whatever happens
choices.feedback: That might cut recall so much that losses rise.

c.text: Week one: complaints spike from blocked genuine customers, and big frauds still slip through.

choices.label: Go back and analyse precision/recall at different thresholds

e.text: Precision is 0.9 but recall fell to 0.35. Fraud losses jump.

d.text: You choose a threshold with recall 0.80 and precision 0.40, add a human-review queue for borderline scores, and monitor weekly. Evaluation became a business decision, not a single number.

quiz.q: TP = 8, FP = 2, FN = 8. Precision?
quiz.why: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 8/(8 + 2) = 0.8. It tells you how many predicted positives were correct.

quiz.q: Same numbers. Recall?
quiz.why: Recall = TP/(TP + FN) = 8/(8 + 8) = 0.5. It tells you how many real positives were found.

quiz.q: Train accuracy 99%, validation 70%. Diagnosis?
quiz.why: A large gap between training accuracy (99%) and validation accuracy (70%) shows overfitting: the model memorised the training data (high variance).

quiz.q: Best metric family when positives are 0.5% of data?
quiz.why: When positives are only 0.5% of the data, accuracy is misleading: predicting all negatives gives 99.5%. Precision, recall or PR-AUC focus on the rare class.

quiz.q: ROC-AUC of 0.5 means…
quiz.why: An ROC-AUC of 0.5 means the model ranks positives above negatives no better than chance. It does not mean 50% accuracy exactly.

questions.q: Supervised learning needs…
questions.why: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples, where the correct answer is given for each input.

questions.q: Predicting a number is…
questions.why: Predicting a number is regression. Classification predicts a category.

questions.q: Which split is for hyperparameter tuning?
questions.why: The validation set is used for tuning hyperparameters. The test set is kept for a final check.

questions.q: k-means needs you to choose…
questions.why: k-means needs you to choose k, the number of clusters, before running it. It is unsupervised, so it needs no labels.

questions.q: Sigmoid of a very large positive number is close to…
questions.why: The sigmoid is 1/(1 + e⁻ˣ). For a very large positive x, e⁻ˣ is close to 0, so the output approaches 1.

questions.q: TP 30, FN 10. Recall?
Fitting the scaler on all data before splitting causes…
questions.why: Fitting the scaler on all data before splitting lets statistics from the test set (mean, spread) influence training. That is data leakage, so scores look better than they really are.

questions.q: Which model family is often strongest on tabular data?
questions.why: Gradient-boosted trees are often the strongest on tabular data. This is a widely seen pattern, but you should still check it on your own data.

questions.q: L1 regularisation tends to…
options: Set some weights exactly to zero
questions.why: L1 regularisation adds a penalty on absolute weight values, which tends to push some weights exactly to zero. This gives sparse models and acts as feature selection.

questions.q: Precision 0.6, recall 0.8. F1?
questions.why: F1 is the harmonic mean: 2PR/(P + R) = 2 × 0.6 × 0.8/(0.6 + 0.8) = 0.96/1.4 ≈ 0.686. The simple average 0.70 is not F1.

questions.q: A model has high error on both training and validation. Best next step?
options: Increase model capacity or add features
questions.why: High error on both training and validation data means underfitting: the model is too simple. Increase capacity or add useful features. More regularisation would make it worse.

questions.q: For forecasting next month's sales, random k-fold shuffling is risky because…
questions.why: For forecasting, random k-fold shuffling puts future data in the training folds, so information from the future leaks in. Use time-based splits, where training is always before testing.

questions.q: Impurity-based feature importance in random forests can be biased toward…
questions.why: Impurity-based importance in random forests can be biased toward high-cardinality features, because they offer many possible split points. Permutation importance or SHAP give a check.

questions.q: Why is MAE often preferred over RMSE for explaining to managers?
options: It is the average error in the original units, less dominated by a few huge errors
questions.why: MAE is the average error in the original units, so it is easy to explain. RMSE squares the errors, so a few huge ones dominate it.

courses.title: Deep learning: neural networks, CNNs, RNNs and transformers
courses.summary: Build intuition and working knowledge of neural networks: neurons, activations, backpropagation and training; convolutional networks for images; recurrent networks for sequences; and the attention mechanism behind transformers.
outcomes: Learners can compute a forward pass and explain how backpropagation and optimisers train a network
Learners can calculate convolution outputs and explain pooling and transfer learning
Learners can explain RNNs, vanishing gradients, LSTMs and embeddings
Learners can compute scaled dot-product attention and distinguish encoder and decoder transformers

lessons.title: Neural networks and how they learn

story.title: Handwritten PIN codes at the post office

scenes.text: At a sorting centre in Nagpur, thousands of envelopes arrive with handwritten PIN codes. Engineer Leela's team wanted machines to read the digits.
Hand-written rules ('a 7 has a horizontal line on top…') failed on messy writing. So they showed a neural network tens of thousands of labelled digit images.
At first it guessed randomly. After each batch, backpropagation nudged millions of weights. After a few passes over the data it read most digits correctly.
Leela still kept a human check for low-confidence envelopes. 'The network is strong, but it should know when it is unsure.'

steps.title: From neuron to network
steps.body:
One **neuron**: z = w · x + b, output a = f(z), where f is an **activation function**.
A **layer** is many neurons side by side: a = f(XW + b). A **deep** network stacks layers: input → hidden layers → output.
Without a non-linear activation, stacked layers collapse into one linear function, so activations are essential.
Common activations:
- **ReLU**: max(0, z) — the default for hidden layers.
- **Sigmoid**: squashes to (0, 1) — binary outputs.
- **Softmax**: turns a vector of scores into probabilities over classes.
- GELU and similar smooth variants are common in transformers.

steps.title: Worked example: a forward pass
steps.body:
x = (1, 2), w = (0.5, −1), b = 1.
z = 0.5×1 + (−1)×2 + 1 = −0.5.
- With ReLU: a = max(0, −0.5) = 0 (the neuron is 'off').
- With sigmoid: a = 1 ÷ (1 + e^0.5) ≈ 0.38.
For a 3-class output with scores (2, 1, 0), softmax gives e²:e¹:e⁰ = 7.39 : 2.72 : 1 → about (0.67, 0.24, 0.09).

steps.title: The training loop
steps.body:
For each mini-batch:
- **Forward pass:** compute predictions.
- **Loss:** cross-entropy for classification, MSE for regression.
- **Backward pass:** backpropagation computes ∂loss/∂w for every weight via the chain rule.
- **Update:** the optimiser (SGD with momentum, Adam, AdamW) changes weights.
One pass over the full dataset is an **epoch**. In PyTorch the core is: optimizer.zero_grad(); loss = loss_fn(model(x), y); loss.backward(); optimizer.step().

steps.title: Making training work
steps.body:
- **Initialisation** matters (He/Xavier schemes keep signals stable).
- **Normalisation** layers (batch norm, layer norm) stabilise training.
- **Regularisation:** dropout (randomly zero activations during training), weight decay, data augmentation, early stopping.
- **Learning-rate schedules:** warm-up then decay.
- Watch training and validation loss curves together.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() → gradients accumulate across batches.
- Leaving dropout on at evaluation time (call model.eval() in PyTorch).
- Applying softmax before a loss that already includes it (PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss expects raw scores, called logits).
- Not shuffling training data; not normalising inputs.
- Trusting a network blindly — it can be confidently wrong on inputs unlike its training data.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Compute softmax of (1, 1, 1) and of (10, 0, 0). What does it tell you about how softmax reacts to large score differences? (Answers: (⅓, ⅓, ⅓) and almost (1, 0, 0).)

activity.prompt: Order one training step of a neural network.
items: Take a mini-batch of examples
Run the forward pass to get predictions
Compute the loss against the true labels
Zero old gradients
Backpropagate to compute gradients
Let the optimiser update the weights
Periodically check validation loss

quiz.q: ReLU(−3) = ?
quiz.why: ReLU(x) = max(0, x). For −3 this gives max(0, −3) = 0.

quiz.q: Why are non-linear activations needed?
options: Without them, stacked layers equal one linear layer
quiz.why: A composition of linear maps is still linear. Without non-linear activations, stacked layers collapse into one linear layer and cannot learn complex patterns.

quiz.q: An epoch is…
options: One pass over the whole training set
quiz.why: An epoch is one full pass over the whole training set, so every example has been seen once.

quiz.q: Dropout is used to…
quiz.why: Dropout randomly switches off neurons during training. This stops them depending on each other too much, so it reduces overfitting.

quiz.q: Softmax of (2, 1, 0) gives the largest probability to…
quiz.why: Softmax gives the largest probability to the largest score. For (2, 1, 0) the first class gets about 0.67.

sources: Standard deep learning texts and framework documentation

story.title: Spotting leaf disease in Karnataka farms

scenes.text: Farmer Mallesh near Mandya noticed spots on his tomato leaves. An agri-tech volunteer, Shreya, photographed them with a phone app.
The app used a convolutional neural network (CNN) fine-tuned from a model pretrained on millions of everyday photos.
It suggested 'early blight, 87% confidence' and advised confirming with the local agricultural officer before spraying.

steps.title: Why convolutions?
steps.body:
A 224×224 colour photo has over 150,000 numbers. Connecting every pixel to every neuron would need enormous numbers of weights and would ignore the fact that nearby pixels belong together.
A **convolution** slides a small **kernel** (filter), e.g. 3×3, across the image, computing a dot product at each position. The same weights are reused everywhere (**weight sharing**), so a 'vertical-edge detector' works anywhere in the picture.

steps.title: Worked example: an edge detector
steps.body:
Kernel (vertical edge): rows [1, 0, −1], [1, 0, −1], [1, 0, −1].
Patch at an edge: rows [10, 10, 0], [10, 10, 0], [10, 10, 0].
Each row: 10×1 + 10×0 + 0×(−1) = 10 → total 30: strong response.
Uniform patch (all 10s): each row 10 − 10 = 0 → total 0: no edge.
In a CNN, kernels are not hand-designed: they are **learned**. Early layers learn edges and colours; deeper layers learn textures, parts (leaf veins, spots) and whole objects.

steps.title: Output size, stride, padding, pooling
steps.body:
Output width = (n + 2p − k) ÷ s + 1, where n = input size, k = kernel size, p = padding, s = stride.
- 32×32 input, k = 5, p = 0, s = 1 → 28×28.
- 'Same' padding (p = 1 for k = 3, s = 1) keeps the size.
- Stride 2 halves the size.
**Pooling** (e.g. 2×2 max-pool) keeps the strongest value in each window, shrinking the map and adding small shift tolerance.
Each kernel produces one **channel** (feature map); a layer with 64 kernels outputs 64 channels.

steps.title: Transfer learning and famous architectures
steps.body:
Rather than training from scratch, take a network pretrained on a large image dataset (such as ImageNet), replace the final layer and **fine-tune** on your smaller dataset — often a few thousand images are enough to get useful results.
Milestones: LeNet-5 (1998, digit recognition), AlexNet (2012, large ImageNet improvement using GPUs), VGG and ResNet (skip connections allowed much deeper networks). Vision transformers (ViT) now compete with CNNs, but CNNs remain common, efficient and well understood, especially on phones.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Dataset bias:** if all diseased photos were taken in the afternoon sun, the model may learn 'lighting', not 'disease'. Check with saliency maps (e.g. Grad-CAM) and test on photos from new farms.
- Data augmentation that changes meaning (flipping digits like 6/9).
- Forgetting to use the same pre-processing (resize, normalisation) as the pretrained model.
- Treating model output as a diagnosis — keep humans and experts in the loop for important decisions.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Compute the output size for a 64×64 input, 3×3 kernel, padding 1, stride 2. (Answer: (64 + 2 − 3) ÷ 2 + 1 = 32.5 → frameworks round down → 32.)

activity.prompt: Input 32×32, kernel 5×5, padding 0, stride 1. What is the output width?

quiz.q: Weight sharing in CNNs means…
options: Every pixel has its own weights
The same kernel weights are used at every position
quiz.why: Weight sharing means the same kernel weights slide over every position of the image. This keeps the number of parameters small and detects a feature wherever it appears.

quiz.q: 2×2 max-pooling on [[1, 3], [2, 0]] gives…
quiz.why: Max-pooling keeps the largest value in the window. The largest of 1, 3, 2, 0 is 3.

quiz.q: Output width for n = 28, k = 3, p = 0, s = 1?
Transfer learning means…
options: Training only the first layer from scratch
Starting from a pretrained model and adapting it
quiz.why: Transfer learning starts from a pretrained model and adapts it to your task. This reuses features it has already learned, so less data and time are needed.

quiz.q: Which innovation let ResNets go much deeper?
quiz.why: ResNets use skip (residual) connections, which add the input to a layer's output. This lets gradients flow easily, so networks can be much deeper.

story.title: Predicting the next word in Hinglish

scenes.text: Aditya built a keyboard app for Hinglish chats ('kal milte hain?'). He needed the model to remember earlier words to predict the next one.
His first recurrent neural network (RNN) forgot the start of long sentences. Switching to an LSTM helped it remember longer.
Later his team moved to a small transformer, which trained faster on GPUs and handled long context better. Understanding RNNs explained *why*.

steps.title: Embeddings: words as vectors
steps.body:
Models cannot read text directly. Text is split into **tokens** (words or word pieces), each mapped to an ID, then to an **embedding** — a learned vector (e.g. 256–4,096 numbers).
Training pushes words used in similar contexts to nearby vectors: 'doctor' near 'nurse'; 'chai' near 'tea'. The famous word2vec observation: vector('king') − vector('man') + vector('woman') lands near vector('queen') — an approximate, not perfect, pattern.

steps.title: Recurrent neural networks
steps.body:
An RNN reads one token at a time and keeps a **hidden state** h — a running memory:
hₜ = tanh(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁ + b)
The same weights are reused at every time step. The final (or each) hidden state feeds a prediction, e.g. the next word or the sentiment of a review.

steps.title: Vanishing and exploding gradients
steps.body:
Backpropagation through time multiplies many factors together, one per time step. If they are mostly smaller than 1, the gradient shrinks towards zero (**vanishing**) and the network cannot learn long-range links; if larger than 1, it **explodes** (fixed with gradient clipping).
Also, RNNs process tokens one after another, so they are hard to parallelise on GPUs.

steps.title: LSTMs and GRUs
steps.body:
The **LSTM** (Long Short-Term Memory, Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a **cell state** and three gates:
- **forget gate:** what to erase from memory,
- **input gate:** what new information to store,
- **output gate:** what to reveal now.
Because the cell state is updated mostly by addition, gradients flow further back. The **GRU** is a simpler variant with two gates. These powered translation, speech and keyboard prediction in the 2010s.

steps.title: Worked example: sentiment from a review
steps.body: Review: 'The food was not good at all'. A bag-of-words model sees 'good' and may predict positive. A sequence model reads 'not' before 'good' and carries that in its hidden state, predicting negative. This order-awareness is why sequence models beat simple word counts on many language tasks.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Multiply 0.9 by itself 50 times (≈ 0.005) and 1.1 by itself 50 times (≈ 117). Relate these numbers to vanishing and exploding gradients over a 50-word sentence.

statements.s: An RNN uses the same weights at every time step.
Vanishing gradients make it hard to learn long-range dependencies.
statements.why: Early tokens get almost no learning signal.
They have forget, input and output gates.

statements.s: Embeddings are fixed by hand and never learned.
statements.why: They are usually learned during training (or pretrained).

statements.s: RNNs are easy to parallelise across time steps.
statements.why: Each step depends on the previous hidden state.

statements.s: Gradient clipping is a common fix for exploding gradients.

quiz.q: What does an RNN's hidden state represent?
options: A running summary of what it has read so far
quiz.why: An RNN's hidden state is a running summary of what it has read so far. It carries memory from one step to the next.

quiz.q: 0.9 multiplied by itself many times shows…
quiz.why: Multiplying 0.9 by itself many times shrinks it towards zero. In backpropagation through many steps, repeated factors below 1 make the gradient vanish.

quiz.q: Which LSTM gate decides what to erase?
quiz.why: The forget gate of an LSTM decides what to erase from the cell state. The input gate decides what to add and the output gate what to expose.

quiz.q: Why does 'not good' confuse a bag-of-words model?
quiz.why: A bag-of-words model ignores word order, so 'not good' becomes just the words 'not' and 'good', and the negation is lost.

quiz.q: A token is…
options: A unit of text such as a word or word piece
quiz.why: A token is a unit of text, such as a word or a piece of a word. Tokenisers often split rare words into pieces, so a token is not always a full word.

story.title: The translator that looked everywhere at once

scenes.text: Meenakshi, a researcher in Chennai, was translating Tamil legal text to English. Older models translated word by word and lost track of long sentences.
A transformer model did better: for each word it produced, it could 'attend' to every source word and weigh which ones mattered most.
She explained to her students: 'Attention is just weighted averaging — dot products, a softmax, and a weighted sum. Everything in modern LLMs is built on it.'

steps.title: Scaled dot-product attention
steps.body:
Each token produces three vectors via learned matrices: a **query** q (what am I looking for?), a **key** k (what do I contain?), and a **value** v (what will I pass on?).
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ ÷ √dₖ) V
- QKᵀ: dot products of every query with every key → relevance scores.
- ÷ √dₖ: keeps scores from growing too large as the vector size dₖ grows (which would make softmax too peaky).
- softmax: turns scores into weights summing to 1.
- × V: weighted average of values.

steps.title: Worked example with tiny numbers
steps.body:
Query q = (1, 0). Keys k₁ = (1, 0), k₂ = (0, 1). Values v₁ = (10, 0), v₂ = (0, 10). dₖ = 2.
- Scores: q·k₁ = 1, q·k₂ = 0 → ÷ √2 → 0.707, 0.
- Softmax: e^0.707 ≈ 2.03, e^0 = 1 → weights ≈ 0.67, 0.33.
- Output ≈ 0.67 × (10, 0) + 0.33 × (0, 10) = (6.7, 3.3).
The query 'paid more attention' to token 1 because its key matched better.

steps.title: The transformer block
steps.body:
Introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al.). Each block has:
- **Multi-head self-attention:** several attention 'heads' in parallel, each free to learn different relations (grammar, coreference, topic).
- **Feed-forward network** applied to each position.
- **Residual connections** and **layer normalisation** around both.
Because attention by itself ignores order, **positional information** is added (sinusoidal encodings, learned positions, or rotary embeddings).
All positions are processed in parallel during training — a big speed advantage over RNNs. The cost: attention compares every token with every other, so compute grows roughly with the square of the sequence length.

steps.title: Encoders, decoders and both
steps.body:
- **Encoder-only** (e.g. BERT, 2018): sees the whole input in both directions; great for classification, search embeddings and extraction.
- **Decoder-only** (the GPT family and most chat LLMs): **causal masking** means each token can attend only to earlier tokens; trained to predict the next token; great for generation.
- **Encoder-decoder** (original transformer, T5): encoder reads the source, decoder generates the target using **cross-attention** — common in translation and summarisation.

steps.title: Common misunderstandings
steps.body:
- Attention weights are not a reliable full explanation of *why* a model decided something.
- Transformers do not 'understand' the way humans do; they learn statistical patterns that can be impressively general and still fail unexpectedly.
- Longer context windows do not guarantee the model uses all the context well; information in the middle of very long inputs can be under-used.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Redo the worked example with q = (2, 0). Do the weights become more or less focused on token 1? (Scores 2 and 0 → ÷√2 → 1.41, 0 → weights ≈ 0.80, 0.20: more focused.)

activity.prompt: Put these milestones of neural networks in order.

events.text: Backpropagation popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams
LSTM introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber
