tech-aws-foundations.title: AWS from zero I: IAM, EC2, VPC, S3 and monitoring
tech-aws-foundations.description: Qwiklabs-style hands-on AWS programme, part 1 of 3: every lesson is a lab - CLI sessions, policy JSON, troubleshooting tickets and console checklists. Goes beyond 'AWS Cloud Practitioner essentials' (tech-cloud-aws-gcp) into associate depth. Tag 'AWS SAA-level' is a topic tag only, not official. All labs are simulated consoles (invented accounts, hosts and IDs) - nothing touches a real cloud. For real practice use each provider's free tier or a sandbox account, and switch on billing alerts/budgets before you start.

courses.title: AWS IAM from zero: users, roles and policies
courses.summary: Hands-on IAM: identities, the policy language, roles for EC2 and cross-account access, and how AWS decides allow vs deny.

lessons.title: Lab: Who am I? Users, groups and the root account

scenes.text: Ananya joins the cloud team. Her manager says: never use the root user; get an IAM identity and MFA.
Her first job: prove which identity her CLI is using and put herself in the right group.

steps.title: Identities in IAM
steps.body:
- **Root user**: the email that created the account. Lock it with MFA, no access keys, use only for a few account-level tasks.
- **IAM user**: long-term identity (avoid for humans in big orgs - prefer IAM Identity Center / SSO).
- **Group**: a bag of users that share policies. Groups cannot be nested and cannot be principals in a policy.
- **Role**: an identity with no password/keys that is *assumed* to get temporary credentials.

steps.title: Know your caller
steps.body: `aws sts get-caller-identity` is the first command of any IAM debugging session: it prints the account and ARN your CLI is really using.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Creating access keys for root.
- Attaching policies directly to dozens of users instead of a group.
- Sharing one IAM user among a team (no accountability in CloudTrail).

activity.prompt: You are in a simulated CloudShell. Confirm your identity, list the groups, add user ananya to the Developers group and verify.

responses.match: /^aws iam add-user-to-group --group-name Developers --user-name ananya$|^aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name ananya --group-name Developers$/

tasks.goal: Show which identity the CLI uses

activity.hint: Try aws iam add-user-to-group --group-name Developers --user-name ananya

quiz.q: Which command shows the identity your AWS CLI is using?
quiz.why: STS GetCallerIdentity works for every identity and needs no permissions.

quiz.q: What should you do with the root user's access keys?
options: Store them in the app config
Share them with the admin team
quiz.why: Root keys are unrestricted; AWS recommends having none.

quiz.q: Can an IAM group be the Principal of a resource policy?
quiz.why: Groups only attach permissions to users; policies name users, roles, accounts or services.

quiz.q: A role differs from a user because a role…
options: can only be used by root
quiz.why: Roles are assumed via STS and give short-lived credentials.

scenes.text: Finance needs a Lambda to read reports from s3://nimbus-reports/monthly/ - and nothing else.
Ananya writes the policy JSON herself.

steps.title: Anatomy of a policy
steps.body: A policy document has `Version` ("2012-10-17") and one or more `Statement`s. Each statement: `Effect` (Allow/Deny), `Action` (e.g. s3:GetObject), `Resource` (ARN), optional `Condition`.

steps.title: Bucket vs object ARNs
steps.body: ListBucket acts on the bucket ARN `arn:aws:s3:::nimbus-reports`; GetObject acts on objects `arn:aws:s3:::nimbus-reports/monthly/*`. Mixing them up is the #1 cause of AccessDenied.

steps.title: Condition keys
steps.body: Limit listing to a prefix with `"Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": "monthly/*"}}`.

activity.prompt: Complete the identity policy so the function can list the monthly prefix and read objects in it.

quiz.q: Which Version string should modern IAM policies use?
quiz.why: 2012-10-17 supports policy variables and is the current language version.

quiz.q: s3:ListBucket must be granted on…
An identity policy is attached to…
quiz.why: Resource policies attach to resources; identity policies to principals.

quiz.q: Least privilege means…
options: granting only the actions and resources needed
quiz.why: Start narrow and widen with evidence.

lessons.title: Lab: Policy evaluation - explicit deny wins

scenes.text: Dev Rohan has AdministratorAccess, yet can't delete a CloudTrail trail.
An SCP from the organisation denies cloudtrail:DeleteTrail.

steps.title: Evaluation order
steps.body:
1. Start with implicit deny.
2. Any **explicit Deny** in any applicable policy (SCP, permission boundary, identity, resource, session) ends it: denied.
3. Otherwise an Allow is needed - and within an account every limiting layer (SCP, boundary, session policy) must also allow.

steps.title: Permission boundaries
steps.body: A boundary sets the *maximum* a user/role can get; it grants nothing by itself.

steps.title: Debugging
steps.body: Use the IAM policy simulator or `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` and read the decoded authorization message.

activity.prompt: Sort each situation by the final decision.

items.text: Identity policy allows s3:GetObject, nothing denies, no SCP limits
Identity allows ec2:*, SCP explicitly denies ec2:TerminateInstances (terminate call)
No policy mentions the action at all
Boundary allows s3:*, identity allows s3:PutObject
Identity allows iam:*, boundary allows only s3:* (iam:CreateUser call)
Bucket policy explicitly denies the user, identity allows

quiz.q: An explicit Deny in an SCP and an Allow in the identity policy gives…
A permission boundary by itself…
quiz.why: Boundaries are a ceiling, not a grant.

quiz.q: If no policy mentions an action, the result is…

steps.title: Trust vs permission policy
steps.body: A role has a **trust policy** (who may assume it - e.g. `ec2.amazonaws.com` or another account) and **permission policies** (what it can do once assumed).

steps.title: Assume a role
steps.body: `aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::210987654321:role/AuditRead --role-session-name audit1` returns AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken and Expiration.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the instance profile (EC2 uses a profile wrapper around the role).
- Trusting an entire account with no ExternalId/conditions for third parties.

lessons.title: Lab: Launch your first instance from the CLI

scenes.text: Nimbus Retail needs a test web server in ap-south-1 before lunch.
Kabir launches it from the CLI so it can be scripted later.

steps.title: What you choose
steps.body: - **AMI** (OS image), **instance type** (e.g. t3.micro: 2 vCPU, 1 GiB), **key pair**, **subnet**, **security group**, **storage**, optional **user data** script.

steps.title: Families
steps.body: t = burstable, m = general, c = compute, r = memory, i = storage-dense, g/p = GPU. The number is the generation; suffix g = Graviton (Arm).

steps.title: Free tier
steps.body: Use a free-tier-eligible type and stop/terminate when done; set a budget alert first.

steps.title: EBS basics
steps.body: EBS volumes live in ONE Availability Zone and attach to instances in that AZ. gp3 gives 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline independent of size; io2 for high, consistent IOPS. Snapshots are incremental and stored regionally.

steps.title: Grow online
steps.body: 1. Snapshot. 2. `aws ec2 modify-volume --size 200`. 3. In the OS: `growpart /dev/nvme1n1 1` (if partitioned) then `xfs_growfs /data` (XFS) or `resize2fs` (ext4).

steps.title: Gotchas
steps.body: You can increase but not shrink a volume. Wait for the modification to reach 'optimizing' or 'completed' before growing the filesystem.

steps.title: CIDR maths
steps.body: A /16 has 65,536 addresses; /24 has 256. AWS reserves **5 addresses per subnet** (network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast), so a /24 gives 251 usable.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: /20 = 2^(32-20) = 4,096 addresses → 4,091 usable in AWS.

steps.body: Never overlap with on-prem or other VPCs you may peer with later - peering and TGW cannot route overlapping CIDRs.

steps.title: What makes a subnet public
steps.body: Only its **route table**: a route 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway (igw-). Private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway (nat-) placed in a *public* subnet.

steps.title: Per-AZ NAT
steps.body: For resilience run one NAT gateway per AZ and point each private route table at its own AZ's NAT.

steps.title: Cost

scenes.text: Users get timeouts on the web tier; a junior engineer 'tightened' a NACL yesterday.
Isha must find out why.

steps.title: The difference
steps.body:
- **Security group**: instance/ENI level, **stateful** (return traffic auto-allowed), allow rules only.
- **Network ACL**: subnet level, **stateless** (return traffic needs its own rule), numbered allow AND deny rules evaluated lowest number first.

steps.title: Ephemeral ports
steps.body: A client reply goes back to a high port (Linux 32768-60999, others 1024-65535). An outbound NACL that only allows 443 breaks responses.

steps.title: VPC Flow Logs
steps.body: REJECT records with the right ports show you which layer dropped traffic.

investigate.label: Read NACL acl-0web on public subnets
investigate.reveal: Inbound: 100 ALLOW 443 0.0.0.0/0. Outbound: 100 ALLOW 443 0.0.0.0/0, * DENY all. Changed 2026-11-25 18:02 by user jr-ops.

investigate.label: Query VPC Flow Logs for REJECT

options: Outbound NACL allows only 443, blocking replies to clients' ephemeral ports
diagnosis.why: NACLs are stateless; responses go to ephemeral ports 1024-65535.

resolution: Raise an emergency change and inform the incident manager
Add outbound NACL rule allowing TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0 before the deny
Confirm Flow Logs show ACCEPT and checkout loads
Add the NACL to IaC with review to prevent drift
Hold a blameless post-incident review

closure.prompt: Write the resolution/closure note for the ticket
closure.model: Root cause: NACL acl-0web outbound change (25 Nov 18:02) allowed only 443, so stateless replies to client ephemeral ports were dropped. Fix: emergency change added outbound rule 110 ALLOW TCP 1024-65535. Verification: Flow Logs ACCEPT, checkout p95 normal. Follow-up: NACLs managed via IaC with peer review.

in order, lowest rule number first

quiz.why: Hence outbound ephemeral rules on NACLs.

steps.title: Versioning

steps.title: Response order

rounds.q: Explain the difference between a security group and a network ACL.
points: allow only vs allow and deny
rounds.model: Security groups attach to ENIs, are stateful and only allow; return traffic is automatic. NACLs apply per subnet, are stateless, evaluate numbered allow and deny rules lowest-first, so you must allow return ephemeral ports. I use SGs as the main control and NACLs as a coarse guard rail, e.g. to block a bad CIDR.
followups: How would you block one malicious IP?

rounds.q: How would you give an EC2 app access to an S3 bucket?
rounds.model: Create a role trusted by ec2.amazonaws.com with a least-privilege policy for that bucket/prefix, wrap it in an instance profile and attach it. The SDK gets temporary credentials from instance metadata, so no keys on disk. I'd verify with aws sts get-caller-identity on the box and test a denied action.

rounds.q: Design a VPC for a two-tier web app across two AZs.
points: public and private subnets per AZ
rounds.model: A /16 with public and private subnets in each of two AZs. ALB in the public subnets, app instances in an Auto Scaling group in private subnets, RDS Multi-AZ in isolated subnets. One NAT gateway per AZ for egress, S3 gateway endpoint, SGs chained ALB→app→DB, Flow Logs on.

rounds.q: An instance fails its instance status check after reboot. What do you do?

I read the system log/console screenshot, look for fstab, kernel or network errors, then fix via EC2 Serial Console or by attaching the root volume to a rescue instance. Then verify 2/2 checks and service health, and record a problem to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: NSG

steps.title: ASGs
steps.body: Application security groups let you write 'asg-web → asg-app:8443' instead of IP lists.

steps.title: VirtualNetwork tag
steps.body: AllowVnetInBound lets everything in the VNet (and peered VNets) in - add explicit denies if you need segmentation.
